name: Abaca
summary: This guide shows how Filipino abaca farmers in Bicol, Eastern Visayas, Davao, Caraga and other uplands usually set up an abaca farm from suckers or corm pieces and care for it until the first stalks are stripped for fiber. It also shows where the usual small farm differs from a well kept one.
season: Plant as the rains begin so the young plants get steady water. Where rain falls well through the whole year, as on the Pacific side of Bicol, Samar and eastern Mindanao, planting can go on in any month. Clearing is best done in the dry months before.
material: Most farmers dig suckers from healthy old mats: immature suckers about 9 to 11 months old and at least 1 m tall take best, while small sword suckers about half a meter tall die more often. Others plant corm pieces (seedpieces) with at least three good eyes, single eye pieces, or tissue culture plantlets bought from a nursery and hardened for about three months. Farmers trim the roots, clean off rotten parts, cut back the leaves and throw out any corm with weevil tunnels, and never take material from a mat with bunchy top or mosaic.
spacing: Square planting, usually 2.5 m by 2.5 m (about 1,600 hills a hectare). 2 m by 2 m to 3 m by 3 m depending on the variety, and 1.5 m by 1.5 m (about 4,000 hills) for varieties that make few suckers. In coconut farms many plant in triangles about 2 m apart. Rows run east to west.
water: Rainfed, on land with rain spread through the year and good drainage. Abaca does not like waterlogged soil. Shade trees and mulch keep the soil damp in the dry months, and some farmers water young plants once or twice a month in summer.
fertilizer: On the usual small farm, little or none: farmers leave dry leaves, cut weeds and stripping waste to rot around the mats. Where they do put fertilizer, it is ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or complete (14 14 14), a little in the hole at planting, more at about 8 months, and complete fertilizer later on, always spread 60 to 90 cm from the plants after ring weeding.
care: Ring weeding about half a meter around each hill, strip weeding along the rows, and underbrushing every month or two on a well kept farm, but only now and then on most farms. Hilling up for more suckers, cutting dry leaves, keeping the shade at about half, and digging out hills sick with bunchy top or mosaic.
harvest: The first stalks are ready at about 16 to 24 months, when the flag leaf appears. After that each mat gives stalks every 3 to 4 months, though many farmers cut only about twice a year. Stalks are topped with a sickle on a pole, felled with a slanting cut, peeled into tuxies the same day, hand stripped with a serrated knife, dried off the ground, bundled with abaca twine and kept dry until sold.

ways.label: Suckers or corm pieces (saha)

steps.title: Clear the land and keep the shade
steps.how: In the dry months, cut the shrubs and grass close to the ground and pile them to rot instead of burning. Keep or plant shade trees such as katuray, anii, dapdap, ipil ipil or coconut, since abaca wants about half shade.
steps.tip: Under coconuts, the coconut trees should stand at least 10 m apart or the abaca gets too dark.

steps.title: Plow where you can
steps.how: Where a plow can get in, as on open land or under coconuts, plow deep one or two times so the soil turns loose and the mat of coconut roots is broken up. On steep land, just clear and dig.

steps.title: Lay out and stake the hills
steps.how: Run straight lines east to west and push a stick about 1 m long where each hill will go, usually in squares of 2.5 m by 2.5 m. Varieties that make few suckers go closer, at 1.5 m by 1.5 m.

steps.title: Dig the holes
steps.how: Dig a hole deep enough for the sucker or corm, putting the dark topsoil on one side and the paler subsoil on the other.

steps.title: Dig and clean the planting material
steps.how: Dig suckers or corms from healthy mats only. Trim the roots, cut away rotten parts and cut back the leaves so the plant loses less water.
steps.tip: Leave out any mat with yellow streaks, bunched leaves or a shrunken top. Those carry virus.

parts.title: Go only to healthy mats
parts.how: Take planting material only from mats of strong, healthy mother plants in a farm free of virus. Walk the mats first and pass by any with yellow streaks, bunched leaves or a stunted top.

parts.title: Choose immature suckers
parts.how: The best suckers are immature ones about 9 to 11 months old and at least 1 m tall. Leave the small sword suckers of about half a meter, which die often after planting.

parts.title: Or cut corm pieces
parts.how: Where suckers are few, dig a healthy corm and cut it into seedpieces that each carry at least three good eyes, or into single eye pieces with one plump bud each.

parts.title: Trim and clean
parts.how: Cut off the old roots and every rotten or dark part, and cut back the leaves so the plant loses less water. Throw out any corm with weevil tunnels in it.

parts.title: Guard against corm weevil
parts.how: Where corm weevil is a problem, many farmers soak the seedpieces or suckers in an insecticide dip before planting.

parts.title: Keep your tools clean
parts.how: Wash and wipe the bolo, knife and spade between mats, since dirty tools carry disease from one hill to the next.

steps.title: Plant and press the soil
steps.how: Put a little fertilizer, with compost if you have it, in the bottom of the hole and cover it with some topsoil. Set the sucker or corm in, fill first with topsoil then with subsoil, and press the soil firm so water does not pool in the hole.
steps.tip: Leave a stick beside every corm or eye piece so you can find it before it sprouts.

steps.title: Replace the missing hills
steps.how: Visit the field two to three weeks after planting and plant again where nothing grew, using immature suckers from healthy mats.

steps.title: Ring weed every month or two
steps.how: Clear the weeds in a ring around each young plant so you can see the hills, and leave the cut weeds to rot as mulch.

steps.title: First fertilizer
steps.how: Between one and three months after planting, scatter fertilizer mixed with compost a little away from the base of each plant, on moist soil.

steps.title: Watch for virus and weevils
steps.how: Walk the farm every month looking for bunchy top, mosaic and bract mosaic, and for aphids on the young leaves. Dig out a sick hill whole, corm and all, and chop it into small pieces so it cannot spread.

steps.title: Hill up and clean the mats
steps.how: Pull soil against the base of each mat with a hoe or spade so it sends up more suckers. Cut off dry leaves and clear the brush between rows.

steps.title: Second fertilizer
steps.how: At about eight months, ring weed first, then spread the fertilizer about 60 to 90 cm away from the plants at the start of the rains, never on dry soil.

steps.title: Cut the mature stalks
steps.how: Cut only stalks whose flag leaf, the last small leaf before the flower, has come out. Cut the leaves first with a sickle tied to a bamboo pole, then fell the stalk with a bolo in a slanting cut about 8 cm above the ground so rain does not sit on the stump.
steps.tip: Stalks that already show fruit are past their best and give weaker fiber.

steps.title: Peel the tuxies the same day
steps.how: Slip a thin knife between the outer and middle layers at the base of each leaf sheath and pull off the outer strips (tuxies), two or three fingers wide, keeping the layers from different sheaths apart.

parts.title: Tuxy within a day of felling
parts.how: Pull the felled stalk apart into its leaf sheaths and take off the tuxies the same day, or within 24 hours at most, before the sheaths turn dark and the fiber loses grade.

parts.title: The locnit way
parts.how: With the sheath still on the stalk, slip the thin tuxying knife between the outer and middle layers at the bottom end, grip the loosened strip and pull it off along the whole length, in two or three strips per sheath.

parts.title: The bacnis way
parts.how: Or first peel the whole sheath off the stalk and split it into two or three pieces as wide as you can handle. Make a slanting cut through the inner layer about 2 feet from the butt end, hold it and pull the inner layer away from the tuxy.

parts.title: Keep the layers apart
parts.how: Pile the tuxies by where their sheath sat on the stalk, outer, middle and inner, since each gives a different grade of fiber.

steps.title: Strip, dry and bundle the fiber
steps.how: Pull the tuxies under the stripping knife within a day. Dry the fiber in the sun for a day or in the air for two to three days, keeping it off the ground, then tie it in bundles and store it dry and raised.

parts.title: Strip under the knife
parts.how: Place each tuxy under the stripping knife on its block, press the knife down and pull the tuxy through with a pulling aid. A knife with no teeth gives the cleanest, best paid fiber, and toothed knives give coarser grades.
parts.tip: Keep the knife teeth even by redenting it now and then, or the grade drops.

parts.title: Hang it in thin layers
parts.how: Hang the wet fiber thinly over bamboo poles on sturdy posts, or lay it on a clean cement floor, keeping the tips off the soil. Turn it over after about two hours.

parts.title: Dry it a day, not longer
parts.how: A day of sun, or two to three days of air drying, brings the fiber dry enough to keep, at about 15 percent moisture or less. Drying much longer makes the fiber brittle and weak.
parts.time: 1 day of sun or 2 to 3 days in air

parts.title: Sort by sheath and color
parts.how: Before bundling, sort the dry fiber by the part of the stalk it came from, how clean it is and its color, and never mix grades in one bundle.

parts.title: Tie the bundles
parts.how: Lay two or three twists of abaca fiber side by side on a clean floor, lay the hanks across them and fold them in half until the bundle is the size you can carry, then tie it tight. Use a twist of the same grade as the bundle.

parts.title: Store it dry and raised
parts.how: Keep the bundles on pallets in a cool, dry shed, away from leaves, twigs and trash. Wrap them in plastic bags when hauling them in the rainy season.

steps.title: Keep cutting every few months
steps.how: Come back every 3 to 4 months to cut the next mature stalks from each mat, so none grows too old and weeds have no room.

ways.note: The first stalks are cut at about 16 to 24 months. After that the same mat is harvested every 3 to 4 months for many years.

mistakes: Taking suckers from mats with bunchy top or mosaic, which spreads the virus to the new farm.
Planting abaca next to corn or beans, which carry the aphids that spread virus.
Planting too few hills a hectare and leaving gaps where mats died.
Weeding and cutting only now and then, so stalks grow too old and the fiber is weak.
Leaving stalks or tuxies overnight before stripping, which spoils the fiber color.
Drying fiber on the bare ground where it gets dirty and moldy.
better: Plant clean suckers or tissue culture plantlets of a good variety from a trusted nursery.
Fill every missing hill and keep the full number of hills a hectare.
Have the soil tested and fertilize on moist soil after ring weeding.
Check the mats every month and dig out virus sick hills at once.
Harvest every 3 to 4 months, cutting only stalks with the flag leaf out.
Strip within a day, dry the fiber well and store it raised in a dry shed.
